extracted.intended_audience: comedy writers, AI/computational-humor researchers, and tech-interested general readers
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and conceptual criteria for building or evaluating systems that autonomously generate jokes from input text (identifying handles, making associations, producing punch lines, and gating output by a score). Describes the Witscript approach and the qualities of contextually integrated, original joke responses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identification of handles (unusual keywords/sentence fragments)
rubrics_metrics.description: The computer identifies the most unusual keywords and sentence fragments in the potential joke topic you uttered. Those are the linguistic elements–I call them handles–that made the topic interesting enough for you to comment on.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: from 'Some airline employee was arrested with over two hundred eighty two thousand dollars in his backpack' the two handles are 'airline employee' and 'two hundred eighty two thousand dollars'. This is likened to IBM Watson decomposing a Jeopardy question into 'subclues.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Generate associations for each handle
rubrics_metrics.description: For each handle the computer generates a list of what I call associations. An association is a word or phrase that’s somehow related to the handle.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: an association of 'airline employee' is 'airport restaurant' with sub-association 'costs a lot of money'; an association of 'two hundred eighty two thousand dollars' is 'a lot of money.' The poster abstract explains using word embeddings to list words associated with keywords. This parallels Watson's 'hypothesis generation' algorithms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Link the best-associated pairs / select strong connections (wordplay selection)
rubrics_metrics.description: The computer makes a connection between two associations and decides to build a punch line around that strong connection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Selection is driven by strength of the connection and 'best wordplay' between association pairs. The Witscript approach explicitly links the two word associations that have the best wordplay to create a punch line.

rubrics_metrics.name: Devise an angle (automated reasoning from topic to punch line)
rubrics_metrics.description: The computer uses its automated reasoning skills to devise what I call an angle leading from the joke topic to the punch line.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example reasoning: 'The airline employee has a lot of money, so he can dine at an airport restaurant, which costs a lot of money.' This is the step that creates the logical/associative path connecting handles to punch.

rubrics_metrics.name: Natural language generation (bridge text and conversational phrasing)
rubrics_metrics.description: The computer uses its natural language generation (NLG) skills to transform the topic-angle-punch line data of the candidate joke into conversational English.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some NLG systems transform numerical data into sentences; Witscript uses a language model fine-tuned on a dataset of jokes to fill the gap between the input text and the punch line with bridge text in a natural-sounding way.

rubrics_metrics.name: Surprise estimation / improbability check (confidence estimation & ranking)
rubrics_metrics.description: The computer decides that the resulting candidate joke is probably surprising enough to be funny by searching through its store of human knowledge and finding that the proposed link is unlikely.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This mirrors Watson's 'confidence estimation' and 'ranking' on candidate answers. Example: the system finds that a meal at an airport restaurant is extremely unlikely to cost $282,000, which supplies the surprise element.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scoring threshold and output gating
rubrics_metrics.description: The system outputs the joke response to the user only if it exceeds a preset score.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Witscript computes a score for candidate jokes and only returns the joke when the score surpasses a preset threshold, i.e., gating output to control quality/relevance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contextual integration / relevance to input
rubrics_metrics.description: Generate original, contextually integrated jokes rather than unrelated or on-request-only jokes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contrast with conversational AIs that only output jokes written by humans, mostly generate nonsense, only tell jokes on request, or tell jokes unrelated to context. Witscript's aim is to produce jokes integrated with the user's input.

rubrics_metrics.name: Originality / independent generation
rubrics_metrics.description: Independently generate original jokes (not merely repeat human-written jokes).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The abstract emphasizes that Witscript 'independently generates original, contextually integrated jokes' as opposed to systems that output jokes written by humans or require heavy human editing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Topic fertility and multiplicity of candidate jokes
rubrics_metrics.description: A fertile joke topic—one with a lot of associations—may spawn three or more different jokes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because multiple association pairs and angles can be found for a rich topic, a system should be able to generate several candidate jokes from one input; multiple acceptable solutions increase chances of producing a laugh.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sufficiency for laughter vs. professional quality (reasonable-funny threshold)
rubrics_metrics.description: Jokes don't have to be of professional quality to get a laugh; they just have to be reasonably funny.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical goal: produce jokes that are 'reasonably funny' to elicit a laugh or comfort (e.g., 'He probably needed the money to buy lunch at the airport.') rather than matching top-tier comedy writing immediately.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of NLP/ML tools and word embeddings as enabling technology
rubrics_metrics.description: Employ natural language processing, natural language generation, machine learning, and word embeddings to identify handles, list associations, and produce bridge text.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author describes learning Python and using off-the-shelf NLP, NLG, and ML tools; the poster abstract explicitly states use of word embeddings to list associated words and a language model fine-tuned on jokes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Human-centered design goal: make AI more engaging via humor
rubrics_metrics.description: Design objective that a system's sense of humor should make the AI appear more human and more engaging to users.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Research shows people prefer to interact with AI that exhibits a sense of humor; a more human computer is more valuable (commercially and for user experience). This justifies optimizing for engagement, not just technical correctness.
